title: In defense of comedic actors and their performances in film

commenti.body: I suppose the Jim Carrey comedies all have Jim Carrey doing his Jim Carrey schtick. Those comedies are more like footage of a comedian being funny. His dramatic roles pull him in different directions, towards different characters. Dramatic performances better befit the medium in that way.

You're spot-on. A lot of dramatic films don't even put much effort into acting, it's all aesthetics. That's never true of comedy, where the actors are pretty much on their own. If you forget about Hollywood and just look at indie films, it seems like the break-out comedies are few and far between. When there's a successful one (like Napoleon Dynamite) it's extremely polarizing to viewers, who focus way more on the performances than they would in a drama.

>Dramatic performances better befit the medium in that way.

How so? Some of the earliest films ever made—even camera tests—are the funniest. Anything could be considered "footage of a comedian," and just replace "comedian" with whatever you want. Footage of a \[method actor\].

I couldn’t agree more. This is a slight detour, but I would go as far as to say people don’t just hate on comedic actors, they hate on comedies.

In recent memory I remember the wave of criticism for Bullet Train for being hollow and goofy, criticism for Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent for not being a deep Charlie Kaufman esque meta narrative, and most prominently, criticism for Don’t Look Up for not being a nuanced and subtle take on the subject and not being more like The Big Short. People hated how hamfisted Don’t Look Up was, but I mean, just because Adam McKay made Vice doesn’t mean he’s not allowed to make unsubtle comedies anymore. People love Step Brothers, but I wonder if it came out after The Big Short in some alternate timeline, if everyone would just dismiss it as “unserious and hamfisted.” These movies are all comedy movies, but true comedies are so rare and so unsuccessful when they do come out that nobody seemed to stop and consider that maybe those movies weren’t trying to be Oscar nominated dramedies like everything else. Maybe they just wanted to be funny popcorn action comedies.

Obviously people want to love comedies. People loved Barbie for instance. But does it take a name director, giant Hollywood stars not known for comedy, old Hollywood homages and feminist speeches for people to go see a comedy movie now? I adored Barbie, but that’s sad if that’s the bar for comedy films because none will ever get made. And it’s okay for movies that primarily just want to get us to laugh to be a bit more vapid than Barbie. That’s not a bad thing.

Not really, because method acting is not a performance piece that people normally seek out, in general.

The Jim Carrey schtick, in this instance, can be found at a comedy club or on SNL or on a sketch show, etc.

You've read my mind. It usually feels like I see so many people wanting to take so many things so seriously, and expect to be challenged thematically when watching movies, including comedies. Not that that's a bad things, considering this sub's identity, but it's not always bad to put all of that to the side and watch something mindless either sometimes.  
  
Ever wonder what one of my personal favorite comedy films is? Hot Rod. Andy Samberg plays a bumbling daredevil who attempts to raise enough money to beat his step-father's cancer so he could defeat him to prove his masculinity to him. It's an totally original, genuinely funny, weirdly wholesome, sometimes absurdist and completely unproblematic comedy that I don't see a lot of people mention nowadays that I've always enjoyed the hell out of. Even when there are attempts at being serious/emotional, it's always undermined with more humor, remaining consistent with its original comedic tone. I miss comedies like this,  and hope that someone in the industry finds a way to bring it back in full swing.

Yeah I’m a hundred percent with you. That being said, I’ve definitely seen some good comedies lately. Mainly action comedies. They just go under appreciated.

D&D was such a great comedy film, and also a great fantasy film, action film, and D&D film. I liked Lost City a lot. Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent which I mentioned was good. An American Pickle. Borat 2. Eurovision. Good Boys. 

I think the problem is short of maybe Borat (a pandemic sequel), Unbearable Weight (advertised as less comedic), and D&D ( a high budget fantasy), nobody really went and saw these.

Even before covid dealt its blow the theaters and the streaming explosion, there amazing comedies coming out that no one went to see. Game Night, Popstar, and Girls Trip are all up there with the best 2000s comedies. 

I think the reasons for this are complex, but one I’ve noticed is the lack of kids going to see movies. When I was in high school, 20 of us would go see the latest blockbuster or comedy movie every week. If there was no blockbuster playing, comedy it is. I don’t think kids can afford that anymore. It was cheap to go the theater back then.

The other thing there is the death of the mall. I’ve never seen this brought up in discussions about theatre attendance before, but it was staggering the sheer amount I used to see movies with my friends on a whim because I was at the mall, or the amount of time we only went to the movie because we knew we could shop around and get out of the house and do dinner for a whole evening. Teens don’t mallrat around anymore, which I think has done a real number on comedy movies specifically

I noticed this changing this year. From M3gan at the start of the year to FNAF at the end of the year, there’s still that young teen audience wanting to go see movies.

But to go to theaters, it has to be justified. It has to be a big film that only works in theaters (Top Gun, Endgame), or an event (Barbenheimer), or in the case of M3gan and FNAF, horror. Horror consistently will bring people in cause it’s way scarier at a theatre.

The draw of dramas in theaters was “see them before the Oscar’s.” Now they always come to streaming before the Oscars. And Oscar viewership is dying. The draw of foreign films was that blockbuster and Netflix didn’t carry them so it was your one chance. Indie films same thing. That’s obviously not an issue anymore.

But I feel like the draw of comedies in theatres was always that you laugh harder with a crowd. I wonder what killed the desire for that specifically. Because I think the poor box office showings on good, funny movies throughout the 2010s is what killed the genre. I mean sure, it was always a genre that made its margins in home video, so it was gonna take a hit. But this hit is drastic. And there were always a few comedies that killed at the box office like The Hangover. Where did they go?

Sorry for not replying sooner, but I think one major factor for this that you didn't mention that others have brought up in the past, is the emergence of short-formed content, People have become more risk-adverse to the types of films they choose to watch in a theater due to increased admission fees and concessions prices, slowly killing the "mid-budget" movie with physical media sales making up a majority of its box office gross. Physical media is also slowly dying simultaneously due to the rise of streaming services, which most newer, modern comedies are being produced and presented on nowadays, especially on YouTube and TikTok, where short-form content is generally prevalent on right now. Malls are dying due to the rapid increases of people shopping online, and short-form content and Internet memes are where kids, mainly within the age range that you and your friends were seeing the latest comedies in the theatres around, get most of their comedy from now. Why spend $10-15 dollars a ticket on something you could get at home for free?  
  
Ever wonder why certain, laugh-a-second comedy films like Airplane, Hot Shots and Naked Gun worked? Because the people behind those films were very talented, smart, and had a great sense of humor altogether, and used those skills in a way to incorporate a great story, timing and pacing, combined with lots of clever visual puns, sight gags, verbal wit and subversive humor to keep everyone who's watching attentive enough to laugh at almost every joke they catch on screen, making for all-around hilarious, timeless and universal comedies. Nowadays, all it takes for a movie to be humorous is to either be self-aware and have characters acknowledge cliches and plot holes (i.e. MCU films, especially Deadpool), have two or more people in a room exchange irrelevant improvisational banter for 5+ minutes in almost every scene (i.e. Judd Apatow and Adam McKay-type stuff), or being crass and juvenile for the sake of being such (i.e. Happy Madison-type stuff). And all of the fast-paced comedic techniques that worked for the ZAZ brothers are now currently being applied to the short-form stuff, with users constantly moving from one comedic short-form video to the next instantly each time.
